title: Jacobo Árbenz Elected President on Reformist Platform
description: Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán won the November 1950 presidential election with over 65% of the vote, succeeding Juan José Arévalo and deepening Guatemala's democratic revolution. His platform centered on agrarian reform, economic nationalism, and reducing dependence on United Fruit Company. The election marked the high point of Guatemala's democratic decade.

title: Decree 900 Land Reform Redistributes 1.5 Million Acres to Peasants
description: The Guatemalan Congress passed Decree 900 on June 17, 1952, expropriating uncultivated land from large estates for redistribution to landless peasants. Approximately 1.5 million acres were distributed to roughly 100,000 families before the 1954 coup reversed the program. United Fruit Company, which held vast tracts of idle land, lobbied Washington aggressively against the reform.

title: CIA Plans Operation PBSUCCESS to Overthrow Árbenz
description: The Eisenhower administration authorized the CIA to plan Operation PBSUCCESS, a covert operation funded at approximately $5–7 million to remove President Árbenz from power. The plan involved training a mercenary force in Honduras and Nicaragua under exiled Guatemalan officer Carlos Castillo Armas, combined with extensive psychological warfare and radio propaganda campaigns.

title: CIA-Backed Coup Overthrows President Árbenz — Operation PBSUCCESS
description: In June 1954 the CIA executed Operation PBSUCCESS: CIA-piloted aircraft bombed Guatemala City while disinformation broadcasts exaggerated the size of the invading force under Castillo Armas. Árbenz, abandoned by his military, resigned on June 27 and went into exile. The coup ended Guatemala's decade of democracy, reversed land reform, and installed the first of a series of U.S.-backed authoritarian rulers.

title: Castillo Armas Seizes Power and Reverses Agrarian Reform
description: Carlos Castillo Armas assumed the presidency after the coup and immediately reversed Decree 900, returning expropriated land to United Fruit Company and the landed elite. He banned the communist party, dissolved Congress, and repressed trade unions. An estimated 70,000 peasant families who had received land under the reform were dispossessed, entrenching Guatemala's extreme land inequality for decades.

title: Castillo Armas Assassinated by Presidential Guard
description: President Carlos Castillo Armas was assassinated on July 26, 1957 by a member of his presidential guard, plunging Guatemala into a political crisis. The motive was never definitively established. Contested elections followed before General Miguel Ydígoras Fuentes assumed the presidency, demonstrating the fragility of the post-coup order.

title: Failed Military Coup Sparks 36-Year Civil War
description: On November 13, 1960, nationalist military officers launched an unsuccessful coup against President Ydígoras Fuentes, partly motivated by resentment over secret CIA training camps for Cuban exile forces on Guatemalan soil. Surviving officers Marco Antonio Yon Sosa and Luis Turcios Lima went underground and formed the nucleus of the FAR guerrilla movement, marking the start of a 36-year civil war that would kill 200,000 people.

title: Military Coup Removes Ydígoras to Prevent Reformist Election
description: Defense Minister Enrique Peralta Azurdia ousted President Ydígoras Fuentes in a coup on March 31, 1963, partly to block former reformist President Juan José Arévalo from running in upcoming elections. The U.S. acquiesced, prioritizing anti-communism over democratic norms. Peralta suspended the constitution and ruled by decree, consolidating the pattern of military political dominance.

title: Forced Disappearance Pioneered as Systematic State Weapon
description: Under the nominally civilian Méndez Montenegro government, Guatemalan security forces first used forced disappearance systematically in Latin America: approximately 28 members of the Guatemalan Workers Party were detained, tortured, killed, and secretly buried in March 1966. The method was later exported to other Latin American dictatorships and became a defining feature of regional Cold War repression.

title: Right-Wing Death Squads Mano Blanca Kill Hundreds of Leftists
description: Paramilitary death squads, particularly Mano Blanca (White Hand), conducted systematic killings of suspected leftists, students, union leaders, and lawyers throughout 1967 with security force complicity. The death squad model became a defining feature of Guatemalan political violence for decades. Combined with army counterinsurgency, an estimated 3,000–8,000 civilians were killed in the late 1960s eastern highlands campaign.

title: General Arana Osorio Elected President, Escalates White Terror
description: Colonel Carlos Arana Osorio, known as the 'Butcher of Zacapa' for his brutal 1966–1968 counterinsurgency campaign, won the 1970 presidential election with military backing. He imposed a state of siege and oversaw massive expansion of death squad activity targeting trade unionists, students, lawyers, and politicians. The violence reached levels one U.S. diplomat described as a 'White Terror.'

title: Presidential Election Fraud Disenfranchises Ríos Montt
description: General Efraín Ríos Montt, the Christian Democratic candidate widely believed to have won the March 1974 presidential election, was deprived of victory by a fraudulent military count in favor of General Kjell Laugerud. The fraud was widely acknowledged. Ríos Montt converted to evangelical Christianity and returned years later to lead the 1982 coup that would make him responsible for genocide against Maya communities.

title: 7.5-Magnitude Earthquake Kills 23,000 and Devastates Highland Communities
description: A massive earthquake struck Guatemala on February 4, 1976, killing approximately 23,000 people, injuring 77,000, and leaving over one million homeless. The indigenous highland departments of Chimaltenango, Quiché, and Huehuetenango suffered the greatest devastation, with traditional adobe housing collapsing catastrophically. The disaster exposed deep inequalities in recovery, with elite urban areas rebuilding far faster than rural indigenous zones.

title: Carter Administration Suspends Military Aid Over Human Rights Abuses
description: The Carter administration suspended U.S. military aid to Guatemala in 1977 under its new human rights policy, citing documented abuses by the security forces. The Guatemalan military defiantly rejected the conditions and turned to Israel and Argentina for military equipment and training. The episode demonstrated both the limits of U.S. human rights pressure and Guatemala's capacity to maintain its counterinsurgency through alternative suppliers.

title: Panzós Massacre: Army Kills Q'eqchi' Maya Land Rights Demonstrators
description: On May 29, 1978, Guatemalan army soldiers opened fire on Q'eqchi' Maya peasants gathered in the town square of Panzós, Alta Verapaz to petition about land rights. Between 35 and 106 people were killed, with many bodies thrown into mass graves. The Panzós massacre galvanized the indigenous rights movement and is considered a pivotal moment that accelerated indigenous communities' alignment with guerrilla opposition.

title: Spanish Embassy Fire Kills 37 Indigenous Rights Advocates
description: On January 31, 1980, Guatemalan security forces stormed the Spanish Embassy occupied by indigenous peasants protesting army massacres in Quiché. The resulting fire killed 37 people including embassy staff and peasant protesters; among the dead was Vicente Menchú, father of future Nobel laureate Rigoberta Menchú. Spain broke diplomatic relations. The massacre became a defining event of the Guatemalan civil war and the impunity crisis.

title: Reagan Administration Restores Support for Guatemalan Military
description: The Reagan administration moved to restore security cooperation with Guatemala after taking office in January 1981, reversing Carter's human rights restrictions. While Congress initially blocked direct military aid, the administration supported Guatemala through third-country channels and restored intelligence sharing. Reagan's backing emboldened the army's counterinsurgency campaign that would reach genocidal scale under Ríos Montt.

title: General Ríos Montt Seizes Power in Coup
description: Junior officers launched a coup on March 23, 1982 against the fraudulently elected president, inviting retired general Efraín Ríos Montt to assume power. Ríos Montt, a born-again evangelical Christian, dissolved the constitution and instituted personal rule. He dramatically intensified the counterinsurgency campaign through scorched-earth operations that the UN's Historical Clarification Commission would later document as genocide.

title: Scorched-Earth Genocide Kills Tens of Thousands of Maya Civilians
description: Under Ríos Montt, the army conducted Operation Victoria 82 and associated offensives targeting indigenous communities in the Ixil Triangle and highland regions. The strategy — drain the sea to catch the fish — involved destroying entire villages, killing civilians of all ages, and burning crops and food stores. The UN's CEH would later document 626 massacres, the majority occurring in 1982–1983, constituting genocide.

title: General Mejía Víctores Overthrows Ríos Montt in Coup
description: Defense Minister Oscar Humberto Mejía Víctores ousted Ríos Montt on August 8, 1983, citing his erratic behavior and evangelical advisors' influence. The scorched-earth campaign continued under Mejía Víctores at diminished intensity. Mejía Víctores initiated a transition toward restricted civilian government, convening a constituent assembly in 1984 that would draft a new constitution.

title: Scorched-Earth Campaign Displaces One Million — Refugees Flee to Mexico
description: The 1982–1983 counterinsurgency campaigns displaced an estimated one million Guatemalans internally, with approximately 150,000 indigenous refugees fleeing to Mexico's Chiapas state. The army resettled survivors in 'model villages' modeled on Vietnam-era strategic hamlets under military control. The mass displacement constituted one of the largest refugee crises in Latin American history at the time.

title: New Democratic Constitution Enacted and Civilian Elections Held
description: Guatemala enacted a new democratic constitution in 1985 providing for multi-party elections and civil liberties. Presidential elections in November 1985 resulted in a victory for Christian Democrat Vinicio Cerezo Arévalo, the first freely elected civilian president in over three decades. However, the military retained substantial autonomy and immunity from human rights prosecutions as unwritten conditions of the transition.

title: Vinicio Cerezo Inaugurated as Guatemala's First Civilian President in 30 Years
description: Vinicio Cerezo Arévalo was inaugurated on January 14, 1986, marking Guatemala's first genuinely civilian government since 1954. Cerezo acknowledged he had perhaps 30% of real power, with the rest remaining in military hands. Despite limited authority, his government established a human rights ombudsman, began tentative peace dialogue with the URNG, and initiated the Esquipulas regional peace process.

title: Esquipulas II Peace Framework Signed by Central American Presidents
description: Guatemalan President Cerezo was a key architect of the Esquipulas II Accord signed in August 1987 by five Central American presidents, providing a regional framework for negotiated peace settlements. The agreement committed signatories to ceasefires, democratization, and national reconciliation. Costa Rican President Óscar Arias won the Nobel Peace Prize for his role; Cerezo's Guatemala hosted key negotiations.

title: Peace Talks Begin Between Government and URNG in Oslo
description: Preliminary peace talks between the Guatemalan government and the URNG guerrilla coalition began in Oslo, Norway in March 1990 under the National Reconciliation Commission. Separate consultations with civil society, business groups, and the military set the stage for formal negotiations. Substantive agreements would not be reached for years, as the process reflected the difficulty of ending a 30-year conflict.

title: Rigoberta Menchú Wins Nobel Peace Prize for Indigenous Rights
description: K'iche' Maya activist Rigoberta Menchú Tum was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in October 1992 for her struggle for social justice and indigenous rights. Her father Vicente had been killed in the 1980 Spanish Embassy fire. The award brought unprecedented international attention to the genocide suffered by Guatemala's Maya communities and created significant pressure on the government to address historical atrocities.

title: Serrano's Self-Coup Fails — Constitutional Crisis Resolved by Civil Society
description: On May 25, 1993, President Serrano dissolved Congress and the Supreme Court in an autogolpe modeled on Fujimori's Peru. Unlike Fujimori, Serrano's move was blocked by civil society protest, business community opposition, the Constitutional Court, and crucially the military, which withdrew support. Serrano fled to Panama and was replaced by Human Rights Ombudsman Ramiro de León Carpio as president.

title: Comprehensive Human Rights Accord Signed with UN Verification
description: The Guatemalan government and URNG signed the Comprehensive Agreement on Human Rights in Mexico City in March 1994, establishing UN verification through MINUGUA. The accord was the first substantive agreement in the peace process and paved the way for subsequent negotiations. MINUGUA deployed throughout Guatemala in November 1994, providing protection for human rights defenders and documenting continuing violations.

title: Comprehensive Peace Accords Signed, Ending 36-Year Civil War
description: On December 29, 1996, the Guatemalan government and the URNG signed the Agreement on a Firm and Lasting Peace, formally ending 36 years of civil conflict that killed approximately 200,000 people. The accords included commitments on indigenous rights, military reform, agrarian reform, and former combatant reintegration. The signing was witnessed by UN Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

title: REMHI Catholic Project Documents 55,000 Cases of War Atrocities
description: The Catholic Church's Recovery of Historical Memory project (REMHI) began publishing its findings in 1997, documenting over 55,000 testimonies of human rights violations. Its four-volume report Guatemala: Never Again attributed approximately 80–90% of atrocities to state security forces and paramilitaries. The report represented the most comprehensive documentation of the civil war's atrocities before the official UN truth commission report.

title: Bishop Juan Gerardi Murdered Two Days After Releasing REMHI Report
description: Monsignor Juan Gerardi Conedera, director of the REMHI project, was bludgeoned to death in his garage on April 26, 1998, two days after presenting the findings to the public. His murder was a direct assault on historical memory and accountability. After years of obstruction, three military officers were convicted in 2001 in the first successful prosecution of Guatemalan officers for a politically motivated killing.

title: CEH Truth Commission Documents Genocide by Guatemalan State
description: The Commission for Historical Clarification (CEH) released Guatemala: Memory of Silence in February 1999, documenting 200,000 deaths, 626 massacres, and over 1.5 million displaced persons during the civil war. The commission concluded that state forces had committed acts of genocide against Maya communities, attributing 93% of atrocities to the army and paramilitaries. The military rejected the genocide finding.

title: Constitutional Referendum on Peace Accord Reforms Fails
description: A constitutional referendum in May 1999 asked Guatemalans to approve amendments required to implement key peace accords commitments, including indigenous rights recognition and military reforms. The referendum failed with only 19% turnout, and the amendments were rejected. The failure dealt a severe blow to peace implementation and reflected both popular apathy and effective mobilization by opponents of reform.

title: Drug Trafficking Expands Rapidly as Guatemala Becomes Key Transit Route
description: Guatemala became an increasingly important cocaine transit corridor from South America to the United States in the early 2000s, with Mexican cartels — particularly the Sinaloa cartel and later the Zetas — establishing operations in the country. Guatemalan police and military were deeply penetrated by trafficking networks. The institutionalization of organized crime in the state apparatus became a defining challenge of the post-war period.

title: Óscar Berger Wins Presidential Election, Defeating Ríos Montt
description: Óscar Berger of the Grand National Alliance won the December 2003 presidential runoff, defeating the discredited Ríos Montt who came third in the first round. Prior to the vote, the Constitutional Court controversially reversed its ruling to allow Ríos Montt — who had seized power in a coup — to run. Berger's victory ended the FRG's hold on the presidency and renewed international confidence in Guatemala's democratic process.

title: Hurricane Stan Triggers Catastrophic Mudslides Killing Over 1,000
description: Tropical Storm Stan struck Guatemala in October 2005, triggering catastrophic mudslides in the western highlands. The Tz'utujil Maya village of Panabaj near Lake Atitlán was largely buried, with hundreds killed and many more missing. Total deaths in Guatemala exceeded 1,000, with thousands more displaced and major infrastructure damage. The disaster disproportionately affected indigenous communities on unstable volcanic slopes.

title: CAFTA Free Trade Agreement Ratified with United States
description: Guatemala ratified the Central America Free Trade Agreement (CAFTA-DR) with the United States in March 2005 after contentious congressional debate. Proponents argued it would attract investment and create jobs; critics feared devastation of smallholder agriculture through competition with subsidized U.S. commodities. The agreement's impacts on rural Guatemalan farmers proved significant, contributing to land concentration and migration acceleration.

title: CICIG Anti-Corruption Commission Established by Guatemala and UN
description: Guatemala and the United Nations signed the agreement establishing the International Commission Against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG) on December 12, 2006. CICIG was given unprecedented authority to investigate clandestine criminal organizations operating within the state, support prosecutions, and reform justice institutions. It represented an innovative model of international-national judicial cooperation against corruption and organized crime.

title: Álvaro Colom Elected — First Center-Left Government Since 1954 CIA Coup
description: Álvaro Colom of the National Unity of Hope won the November 2007 presidential runoff, representing Guatemala's first center-left government since the CIA overthrew Árbenz in 1954. Colom emphasized social spending, conditional cash transfer programs for poor families (Mi Familia Progresa), and engagement with indigenous communities. His election was a significant symbolic milestone in Guatemalan politics.

title: Dos Erres Massacre Case: Former Kaibiles Convicted and Sentenced
description: The Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled against Guatemala in the Dos Erres case, ordering accountability for the 1982 massacre where Guatemalan Kaibil special forces killed approximately 250 civilians in Petén. Subsequent domestic prosecutions of former Kaibiles resulted in convictions and sentences of over 6,000 years in prison each. The landmark verdicts, including extraditions from the United States and Canada, advanced genocide accountability.

title: Double Disaster: Tropical Storm Agatha and Pacaya Volcano Eruption
description: In May 2010, Guatemala suffered simultaneous disasters: Tropical Storm Agatha triggered massive flooding and mudslides killing over 150 people while Pacaya volcano erupted, forcing evacuations near the capital. A dramatic sinkhole 60 feet wide also opened in Guatemala City. The coinciding disasters overwhelmed emergency response capacity and highlighted Guatemala's extreme vulnerability to multiple simultaneous natural hazards.

title: Otto Pérez Molina — Former Military Intelligence Chief — Elected President
description: Otto Pérez Molina of the Patriot Party won the 2011 presidential election on an 'iron fist' anti-crime platform, becoming Guatemala's first military general to win a democratic election. Pérez Molina had been chief of military intelligence during the civil war and was named in human rights reports. His election was seen by many as the military's return to formal political power through democratic means.

title: Ríos Montt Convicted of Genocide — Verdict Annulled Ten Days Later
description: On May 10, 2013, a Guatemalan court convicted 86-year-old Efraín Ríos Montt of genocide and crimes against humanity, sentencing him to 80 years in prison — the first time a former head of state had been convicted of genocide by his own country's courts. However, the Constitutional Court annulled the verdict ten days later on procedural grounds in a deeply politicized decision. Ríos Montt died in 2018 before a final verdict.

title: El Niño Drought Devastates Dry Corridor Smallholder Farmers
description: A severe El Niño-driven drought devastated subsistence agriculture in Guatemala's eastern Dry Corridor in 2014, causing crop failures among smallholder corn and bean farmers. Hundreds of thousands were pushed toward food insecurity, contributing to a surge in migration toward the United States. The crisis highlighted the climate vulnerability of Guatemala's agricultural poor and the inadequacy of social protection systems.

title: La Línea Scandal Topples President Pérez Molina After Mass Protests
description: In April 2015, CICIG and the Attorney General revealed La Línea — a customs fraud network siphoning millions from import duties — with wiretap evidence directly implicating President Pérez Molina and Vice President Roxana Baldetti. Hundreds of thousands marched weekly under #RenunciaYa. Baldetti resigned in May; Pérez Molina resigned on September 3 and was arrested the next day in Guatemala's most significant accountability moment in decades.

title: Jimmy Morales Elected President on Anti-Corruption Wave
description: Television comedian Jimmy Morales of the FCN-Nación party won the October 2015 presidential runoff on the slogan 'Neither corrupt nor a thief,' capitalizing on anti-corruption sentiment following the Pérez Molina scandal. His party had deep ties to former military officers — a connection that would define his later confrontation with CICIG when the commission investigated him and his family for illicit campaign financing.

title: Morales Attempts to Expel CICIG Commissioner — Constitutional Court Blocks It
description: President Morales declared CICIG Commissioner Iván Velásquez persona non grata and attempted to expel him in August 2017, shortly after CICIG filed campaign financing charges against Morales. The Constitutional Court blocked the expulsion order. The confrontation marked the beginning of an escalating conflict between Morales and the anti-corruption commission that would define the remainder of his presidency.

title: Volcán de Fuego Eruption Kills Nearly 200 in Pyroclastic Flows
description: Volcán de Fuego erupted on June 3, 2018, sending pyroclastic flows through communities on its slopes and officially killing nearly 200 people, with local estimates suggesting far higher casualties. The village of San Miguel Los Lotes was completely buried. The death toll was amplified by inadequate early warnings and evacuation delays. It was Guatemala's deadliest volcanic disaster in decades and sparked controversy over emergency response failures.

title: CICIG Formally Closes After 12 Years of Anti-Corruption Work
description: The International Commission Against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG) formally ended operations in September 2019 after President Morales refused to renew its mandate. Over 12 years CICIG had secured over 300 convictions and dismantled numerous criminal networks within state institutions. Its closure was widely condemned as a major setback for rule of law, and many prosecutors who worked with CICIG were subsequently forced into exile.

title: Alejandro Giammattei Wins Presidential Election
description: Conservative physician Alejandro Giammattei of the VAMOS party won the August 2019 presidential election, defeating Sandra Torres. His administration was marked by systematic attacks on independent prosecutors and judges, corruption allegations, and poor management of the COVID-19 pandemic. Giammattei's government also signed a controversial 'safe third country' asylum agreement with the United States under Trump administration pressure.

title: Anti-Corruption Protesters Set Fire to Congress Over Budget Scandal
description: In November 2020, thousands of Guatemalans took to the streets after Congress secretly passed a budget that tripled legislators' salaries while cutting social spending including COVID-19 and hurricane relief funds. Protesters broke into and set fire to part of the Congress building. The protests reflected deep public anger at corruption and elite impunity. President Giammattei vetoed the budget under popular pressure.

title: Hurricanes Eta and Iota Cause Catastrophic Flooding in November
description: Back-to-back Category 4 hurricanes — Eta and Iota — struck Central America within two weeks in November 2020, causing catastrophic flooding and landslides across Guatemala. Alta Verapaz and the Polochic Valley were particularly devastated with death tolls exceeding 100 and hundreds of thousands affected. Recovery was complicated by COVID-19 restrictions and pre-existing poverty, compounding an already acute humanitarian crisis.

title: Anti-Corruption Prosecutor Juan Francisco Sandoval Fired and Flees to Exile
description: Attorney General Consuelo Porras fired anti-corruption prosecutor Juan Francisco Sandoval on July 23, 2021. Sandoval fled to El Salvador hours later citing safety concerns. His dismissal was internationally condemned as an attack on judicial independence. The Biden administration placed Guatemala on the 'Engel List' of corrupt officials and those undermining democracy, and Sandoval was later granted asylum in the United States.

title: Systematic Persecution of Anti-Corruption Prosecutors and Judges
description: Guatemala's anti-corruption legal community faced systematic persecution in 2022, with dozens of prosecutors and judges pressured, charged with crimes, or driven into exile. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights granted precautionary measures to numerous Guatemalan justice operators. In exile, former FECI prosecutors established networks to continue documenting corruption and supporting international accountability mechanisms.

title: Remittances Exceed $18 Billion Annually — Over 18% of GDP
description: Remittances sent by Guatemalan migrants living abroad — primarily in the United States — surpassed $18 billion in 2022, equivalent to over 18% of GDP and exceeding all other sources of foreign exchange including exports. Communities throughout the western highlands became structurally dependent on remittance income, reflecting the transformation of migration from individual survival strategy to an economic pillar of the national economy.

title: Bernardo Arévalo Wins Presidential Election on Anti-Corruption Platform
description: Bernardo Arévalo of the Semilla party unexpectedly advanced to the second round of Guatemala's June 2023 presidential election with 11.8% of the vote, then won the August runoff against Sandra Torres with approximately 58%. Running explicitly on an anti-corruption platform, his victory was celebrated internationally as a democratic breakthrough. His election was the first time a genuinely reformist candidate had won since the 1950s.

title: Attorney General Attempts to Annul Semilla Party and Block Inauguration
description: Following Arévalo's electoral victory, Attorney General Consuelo Porras and prosecutor Rafael Curruchiche launched an unprecedented campaign to annul the Semilla party, raiding the Supreme Electoral Tribunal and seizing ballot materials. The actions were condemned internationally as an attempted judicial coup by the OAS, EU, and United States. The actions failed to block the inauguration but illustrated the depth of state capture by corrupt networks.

title: Indigenous Communities Hold 100-Day Blockade in Defense of Democracy
description: Indigenous Maya, Xinca, and Garífuna communities organized a nationwide protest movement lasting over 100 days beginning in October 2023 — including 142 simultaneous road blockades — demanding Arévalo's inauguration and Attorney General Porras's resignation. Led by the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán, the movement was a historic assertion of indigenous political agency and became internationally recognized as decisive in preserving Guatemala's democratic outcome.

title: Bernardo Arévalo Inaugurated as President After Chaotic Transfer of Power
description: Bernardo Arévalo was inaugurated as President of Guatemala on January 15, 2024, after a chaotic night in which the outgoing Congress delayed proceedings for hours in apparent efforts to complicate the transfer of power. His inauguration — celebrated by crowds and international representatives — was seen as a defense of democratic governance against an entrenched corrupt elite. Arévalo immediately announced anti-corruption reforms as his primary agenda.

title: Arévalo Government Faces Systematic Institutional Blockades from Prosecutors
description: Throughout 2024, the Arévalo government faced systematic obstruction from the Attorney General's office and allied judges, who continued prosecuting Semilla party officials and impeding government appointments. The confrontation illustrated the depth of capture of state institutions by corrupt networks and the difficulty of reform within a captured state. Guatemala's democratic crisis attracted international attention as a test case for anti-corruption governance.

title: Arévalo Government Pursues Anti-Corruption Reforms Amid Continued Obstruction
description: President Arévalo's government continued advancing anti-corruption measures in 2025, including civil service reform, transparency initiatives, and engagement with international accountability partners. The attorney general's office remained a major institutional obstacle, but the government maintained broad popular support. Guatemala's democratic resilience — demonstrated in the 2023 election crisis — attracted international attention as a potential model for resisting democratic backsliding.

title: Banco Metropolitano and Banco Promotor Interventions Threaten Systemic Risk
description: Guatemala's Monetary Board intervened Banco Empresarial on February 9, 2001, then administratively intervened Banco Metropolitano and Banco Promotor on March 1, 2001 due to severe liquidity and solvency problems, explicitly authorizing contingency credit lines to contain potential systemic risk. On June 7, 2001 the Superintendent of Banks also took control of Financiera Metropolitana after it suspended payment of its obligations. Regulators ultimately concluded the three banks could not continue operating and moved them into liquidation.
